notes.title: News – Performance & Auto-Saving
notes.notes:
Hey Steam!

I've updated the demo with some performance improvements and a fully reworked auto-saving system.

Overall framerates should be better, and you'll have more options to tweak low / medium / high settings to your preference – like the option to turn Lumen, Reflections or even AA off completely.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/3563110/The_Button_Effect__Demo/
Auto-saving is now much lighter and will store all of your steps – in case of a crash or unexpected power outage, it will reload your progress and store a back-up of the previous save file on the next play.

I've also added a few smaller QoL changes, like increasing the range of the Sensitivity slider for better control and adding a Brightness slider for devices with darker screens.

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2299940/view/536612324936517612?l=english]For a complete list of changes check out the patch notes: Demo Update 0.1.5[/url]

Looking ahead, I'll be focusing on new puzzle content and level designs for the mid- and endgame – I'm excited for you to solve what's coming!

Thank you for all of your feedback, patience and support – it helps me make a better game.
-Tim ([url=https://store.steampowered.com/developer/frycandle]Frycandle[/url])

notes.title: Demo Build - Update 0.1.5
notes.notes:
Several performance improvements to the Steam Demo build.

In the past months I've been focusing on performance improvements to address some of the issues players were having on low/medium and high setups. Framerates should now be improved on all presets, especially allowing more options to be tweaked for low and medium setups. I've also completely reworked the saving system with more performant autosaving to reduce framedrops.

(!) Note: If you're playing on an older save from 0.1.4 or earlier, you'll have to toggle between the quality presets or reset to default video settings to apply the new changes correctly.

(!) Note: If you're playing on an older save from 0.1.4 or earlier the autosaving will still default to the less performant saving method to ensure backwards compatibility. Fresh saves use the new system.

Changes:
- Reworked Low / Medium / High quality presets
- Added a Global Illumination option to turn Lumen off completely on lower end hardware
- Added TSR / TAA / FXAA / NO AA Anti Aliasing options to the video settings menu
- Added and optimized CSM / VSM Shadow settings
- Added and optimized Off / SSR / Lumen options for Reflections
- Added Texture resolution settings
- Added a new Brightness setting slider to brighten dark or hard to see areas on certain screens
- Added ceiling lights to darker areas in the lower level to help with navigation
- Reduced and cleaned up files sizes, materials, engine settings, redundant code and more
- Optimized clouds and other elements in the environment
- Optimized and reworked performance intensive blueprints
- Optimized and reworked auto-saving to reduce hitches on new saves
- Changed the default Steam Deck preset to Low for 60 FPS (Medium runs at 30-40 FPS)

Bugs:
- Fixed an issue where setting Global Illumination to Medium made certain areas in the game too dark and hard to see. Medium (Lumen) is now the default for increased performance.
- Fixed an issue where screen fade transitions would not cover the full screen on 21:9 monitors
- Fixed an issue where the lowest mouse sensitivity would still be too sensitive. Increased the mouse sensitivity slider range for more control.

Updated Minimum Requirements:
- GTX 1050 Ti / 4GB VRAM for 60 FPS on Low settings
- DirectX Version 12 is required
- Integrated Intel GPUs are not supported

If you had performance issues before, or an older graphics card, let me know if these new options made a difference on your machine. Sharing your preset (low/medium/high), your FPS (displayed in the video settings menu) and your graphics card with me would be very helpful.

I'll try to further improve the performance as development progresses.

notes.title: Devlog – Puzzle Design Process
notes.notes:
Hey Steam!

Welcome to all the new puzzlers here from Reddit, you've helped me and my game reach 2000 wishlists and nearly 100 followers here on Steam! Thank you for your support, it helps!

[hr][/hr]
The comments on my Reddit post were genuinely kind and supportive. One of those comments was an interesting question about the game's puzzle design and my process:
 
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45292736/9a88db27e7e6485b4878bc6fe3755ddef4d2e23a.png[/img]

This devlog answers that question. If you're short on time though, here's what I replied:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45292736/fa54772a3030e461fc382880ab84f2c60e821601.png[/img]

That's the short answer. but I wanted to elaborate on this because the process of [i]'coming up with the puzzles'[/i] is one of the most fulfilling aspects of game development for me. It's one of the tasks I could do for hours on end, happily, and completely lose track of time. It triggers my perfectionism and curiosity to keep going until I've found the most interesting solution or interaction.

I have to thank Patrick Traynor (Patrick's Parabox) for a lot of this. When I first started making puzzle games about 2 years ago, his [url=https://cwpat.me/misc/puzzle-level-idea-strategies/]article[/url] helped me find puzzle design strategies that work for me.

[hr][/hr]
The most important part (for me) is endless iteration. It's a curious process of playing around with ideas for mechanics and puzzles, observing the consequences, and keeping an eye out for interesting interactions you might not have expected to happen. With some effort and polish, 'happy accidents' can become solutions to a puzzle or a-ha moments in the final game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45292736/56a180e53a4c9e377271d6fd0cdf69467a2b1173.png[/img]
[i]Screenshot: Prototype levels with dozens of iterations and variations (for a handful of puzzles)[/i]

Most of the work that goes into it will never be seen. (see screenshot) For every 50 puzzle drafts, only a handful will make it into the final game. In summary this is how I approach puzzle design:

[b]Inspiration:[/b] Take inspiration from programming, architecture and life to generate ideas
[b]Prototype:[/b] Prototype the basic building blocks to be able to validate and explore those ideas
[b]Experiment:[/b] Playfully combine and experiment with mechanics and interactions
[b]Iterate, Iterate, Iterate:[/b] Focus on the most interesting results and thoroughly explore them
[b]Curate:[/b] Collect and select the most interesting puzzles
[b]Polish:[/b] Play-test and polish the selected puzzles

[hr][/hr]
In a way, designing puzzle games is a lot like playing them! It's a playful process that requires you to test your assumptions and ask yourself the right questions to come up with new solutions.

Speaking of playing them... [b]I'll be releasing a Steam demo in the next few months![/b]

Have a great weekend,
-Tim ([url=https://store.steampowered.com/developer/frycandle]Frycandle[/url])

notes.title: Devlog – Crouch and Zoom
notes.notes:
Hey Steam!

The most requested feature from a recent play-test session: [i]Crouch[/i].

I'm constantly testing the game to improve it based on player feedback. One of the bigger play-test sessions (~20 play-testers playing the same build) had an overall positive response, plus constructive feedback to improve the experience. Wanting to crouch was mentioned by almost every single tester.
[hr][/hr]
When I first started developing the game I aimed to keep the controls as simple as possible.
[i]
WASD / Arrow keys = Move
Left-click = Interact
Shift = Speedwalk[/i]

In one of the earliest builds I had enabled a tiny jump (Spacebar), but there wasn't a single reason or function to the jump. I didn't want jumping over/on top of puzzles to be a requirement anywhere since it's a skill focused on agility and timing, so I ended up scrapping jump entirely.

I had considered crouch in the past as it has the potential to open up new perspectives and viewpoints to approach or see a puzzle from a new angle. I decided to test it out by adding both crouch and zoom.

[i]CTRL = Crouch
Right-click = Zoom[/i]

Huge improvement! These changes, while small, completely open up the game:

[previewyoutube=iBXYKcqbGLA?vq=hd1080;full][/previewyoutube]

Why? Understanding and perceiving [spoiler]line of sight[/spoiler] is key to solving many of the puzzles in the game. Being able to crouch and lower yourself to the height of certain buttons is a game-changer.

It also adds lots of potential for [spoiler]secret buttons[/spoiler] that can only be seen from certain angles...

Zoom helps by allowing you to zoom ahead into the levels if you can't quite see what's in the next corridor, or if you want to solve a puzzle from a distance and increase your potential FOV.
[hr][/hr]
What do you think of these new controls? Would you prefer 'hold to crouch' or 'toggle'?

Thanks,
-Tim ([url=https://store.steampowered.com/developer/frycandle]Frycandle[/url])

notes.title: Frequently Asked Questions
notes.notes:
Hey Steam!

Thanks for following along, wishlisting the game and sharing my announcement! With your help, the game has managed to hit nearly 1000 [i](988)[/i] wishlists in the first two weeks.

On top of this, I've felt the support from fellow developers and the Thinky Games community:
[list]
[*] [url=https://x.com/Demruth/status/1855050367203262866]Alexander Bruce quote re-tweeted my game[/url]
[*] [url=https://www.twitch.tv/j_blow]Jonathan Blow streamed the game on his Twitch channel[/url]
[*] [url=https://thinkygames.com/games/the-button-effect/]Thinky Games covered and added the game to their database[/url]
[/list]
Shout-out to Davor Hunski [i](The Talos Principle)[/i], Albert Shih [i](Superliminal)[/i], Elyot Grant [i](Islands of Insight)[/i], Patrick Traynor[i] (Patrick's Parabox)[/i], Le Slo [i](Alephant)[/i], Matthew VanDevander [i](Taiji)[/i], Alan Hazelden [i](Draknek)[/i], Nozomu [i](Robot Detour)[/i], Thomas Mackinnon[i] (THE CORRIDOR)[/i], Tad Cordle [i](Sensorium)[/i] and many more for play-testing early builds of the game.
[hr][/hr]
This is my first devlog after over a year of development. As a developer, I'm a bit torn on what I should or shouldn't share in terms of game design/mechanics. The game is all about rule discovery and mastering mechanics over time, I don't want to spoil or ruin that experience for you.

Anything that might be considered a spoiler, like this [spoiler]spoiler example[/spoiler], will be marked as a spoiler. If you want to go in blind, [spoiler]don't hover over these[/spoiler]!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45292736/77bfa9e8d9989669ab48f9dfefa9322cf88e6557.png[/img]
I'll be posting a devlog every month or so, depending on my schedule. I'd love to share interesting bits and pieces of my process along the way. What would you prefer to see (or not see) in a devlog for a puzzle game that's in active development?
[hr][/hr]
Let's start simple by giving you an overview of where I'm at:
[list]
[*] Late 2022: I joined a game-jam that triggered the idea to hyperfocus on the button mechanic
[*] February 2023: I developed a rough prototype next to my work as an architectural engineer
[*] March 2023: I reduced my engineering hours to a minimum to make time for game development
[*] May 2023: I applied for the Astra Fellowship grant but didn't make it through final selections
[*] July 2023: I continued to improve my early demo and asked for advice from fellow developers
[*] October 2023: I became increasingly unhappy in my engineering job and quit (not recommended)
[*] Late 2023: I continued to self-fund pre-production and prepared pitches to find funding
[*] April 2024: I sent in my pitch to the Dutch equivalent of Indie Fund (a dev friendly initiative)
[*] May 2024: I succesfully received funding from Midgame Fund to fund my project full-time
[*] June 2024: I quietly showcased a build of the game at the INDIGO showcase in Utrecht (NL)
[*] August 2024: I focused on improving the game's visuals, trailer and store-page materials
[*] November 2024: I announced the game and published the Steam store-page
[/list]
My next milestone? – Work towards a playable Steam demo!

I'm also focusing on production: I've got new mechanics to explore, puzzles to design and levels to tie together. Significant amounts of my time go into iteration – which I believe is worth it in the long run. I prefer quality over quantity, only the most interesting designs should make it into the final game.

More on that later. Let me know what you'd like to see?
[hr][/hr]
For now, let's wrap up this somewhat lengthy devlog with a short FAQ:

(Q) [u]How long will the game be?[/u]
[i](A) 3~4 hours is the current estimated playtime[/i]

(Q) [u]What are the target platforms?[/u]
[i](A) Windows (PC) only at first, potentially Steam Deck and Linux/MacOS after[/i]

(Q) [u]How do you design puzzles using nothing but buttons?[/u]
[i](A)[spoiler]Each of the various button types has its own hidden ruleset[/spoiler][/i]

(Q) [u]What will it cost?[/u]
[i](A) It depends on the content, but likely somewhere between $9,99 ~ $19,99[/i]

(Q) [u]Is the music inspired by Westworld?[/u]
[i](A) Not intentionally, I sent my composer Beth's Story (The Queen's Gambit) as a reference[/i]

[hr][/hr]
That's all for now. If you're curious about specific aspects of the game, feel free to ask me anything!

Thanks for reading,
-Tim ([url=https://store.steampowered.com/developer/frycandle]Frycandle[/url])

notes.title: The Button Effect – Game Announcement
